#### **LME warehouse queues and their impact on metals markets** 

- Waiting times of close to a year for delivery of metal have emerged at three LME warehouse locations.  A further two have queues of greater than ten weeks.  This article seeks to explain why such queues have developed and examines the impact of material not being readily available on the various LME metals markets.  It also considers potential future developments. 

- It is the volume and concentration of stocks in certain locations that causes queues.  Of the LME metals, only aluminium and zinc are currently held in sufficient volumes to cause lengthy delays to deliveries.  But it is not just the volume of material that is important.  The concentration of aluminium and zinc in just a few locations, in combination with their large volume, has led to a situation in which demand for these metals is greater than the rate at which metal is delivered out. 

- Other metals can be caught within these queuing systems too.  There are no separate delivery streams for different metals, so a queue at a warehouse will affect all metals held at that location.  The queues act to temporarily limit the availability of physical metal, even if stocks are high.  In turn, this places upward pressure on regional merchant premiums. 

- Although copper has been relatively unaffect

ed by these stock developments to date, there have been concerns that this could change. Until now, the copper market has been supply-constrained as new projects and expansions have been delayed and the industry has suffered from a high level of supply disruption. The global volume of copper stocks has consequently remained low and only a small percentage has been held in LME warehouses. But with fewer than usual disruptions this year and the likelihood of market surpluses in the future, there is a question over whether copper too will become subject to LME queues and escalating premiums. © 2012 CRU International Limited **confidential** Page 1 of 16 November 2012 Copper Studies www.crugroup.com #### **Queues emerge at LME warehouses for metal to be delivered out** On 9 November 2012 LME approved warehouses at New Orleans held 49,750t of copper, almost 30,000t of which was cancelled tonnage. Just 75t of copper was delivered out of New Orleans that day. Almost 65,000t of aluminium and 385,000t of zinc were also waiting to leave New Orleans warehouses that day, of which a total of 3,900t were delivered out. At this rate it would take 123 working days to clear the backlog. Similarly lengthy waits for physical metal from LME warehouses have emerged elsewhere, with Detroit in the USA and Vlissingen in the Netherlands being prominent examples. Such was the wait at Vlissingen that the LME delisted it as a location for copper storage in April 2012 in order to prevent too large a quantity of copper stocks being kept from physical delivery for extended periods. Since 2008, total stocks in LME warehouses have increased almost sevenfold to reach just under 7Mt. This has been largely driven by the increase in aluminium stocks from less than 1Mt in January 2008 to over 5Mt in November 2012. This is not a problem in itself, however, it has contributed to a situation in which queues to take material out of warehouses have increased. Long waits to receive aluminium from warehouses after warrants have been cancelled has distorted the market. Warehouses are able to attract metal by offering incentives while remaining confident of receiving many weeks or months of rental income even after a warrant has been cancelled. This can make supply seem artificially tight and result in premiums for physical metal increasing sharply. In addition, forward selling, in order to take advantage of a sizeable contango, or financing deals, where the metal is used as collateral for a loan, may contribute to the tightness by leading to an increase in LME stocks and tying-up material away from the physical market. Although it is the aluminium market that has been mainly affected by these warehousing issues so far, the markets for all LME metals have the potential to be affected, as each lot of metal has to wait in a queue for its turn to leave the warehouse. © 2012 CRU International Limited **confidential** Page 2 of 16 November 2012 Copper Studies www.crugroup.com #### **Rental charges incentivise warehouses to hold onto stock...** Globally there are over 700 LME approved warehouses across 37 locations in 14 countries. Concerns have been voiced about the ownership of a large number of warehouses by a few large players, which are in turn owned by major banks and trading houses such as Glencore (Pacorini), Trafigura (NEMS), Goldman Sachs (Metro), and JP Morgan (Henry Bath). Our research, however, suggests that ownership per se has had no impact on the formation of warehouse queues and rising premiums. Warehouse revenues come from rental rates (a daily rate per tonne of material) and an FOT (free on truck) charge when the material leaves the warehouse. The FOT charge is a one-off charge, which can provide a disincentive for owners to remove material from a warehouse. Rental rates incentivise the warehouse company to keep metal in the warehouse for as long as possible. These rates vary between warehouses, with the maximum rent charged by warehouses for copper ranging between 36 and 41 cents per tonne per day, a difference of $1.25 per 25 tonne lot of copper each day. In reality warehouses may offer discounts and other incentives to attract metal. With growing queues to get metal out, warehouses can offer larger incentives in the knowledge that total revenue from rental income will remain high. For those putting metal into warehouses, the location chosen will, at least in part, depend on what the cheapest location is for their specific needs. A warehouse user will aim to make use of a warehouse where the combination of anticipated rental charges and the FOT charge is lowest for them. Traders may also seek to store material at their own warehouses, thus keeping storage costs ‘in-house’. A challenge does, however, arise when it comes to purchasing metal in a specific location rather than a contract on the LME. Futures contracts traded on the LME do not show any location information; but warrants themselves are location and metal-type specific. Trade in warrants, through brokers, enables those seeking physical metal to obtain it in the location and shape required. Certain warrants, the most desirable, trade at a premium – so in some instances it may be more expensive to obtain metal from a warehouse with a short queue, or with a low rental charge. #### **...but warehouse rules have greater influence on development of queues** Warehouses must meet a number of criteria and adhere to certain rules to become LME approved. Most important when looking at the queues that have formed at certain warehouse locations is the ‘minimum load-out rate’. This sets the minimum amount of metal that a company’s operations at a g

iven location must deliver out in a single day.  As warehouses make money from per day rental charges, even when a warrant has been cancelled and material is waiting in a queue to leave the warehouse, there is no financial incentive to exceed this minimum.  The ‘minimum’ from the LME’s perspective is, in essence, a maximum from a warehouse perspective. 

Prior to 1April 2012, the minimum load-out rate was based on a company’s capacity in a given location and rose to a maximum of 1,500t per day.  In response to the growing queues, the LME increased the minimum rate to 3,000t per day for companies with over 900,000t stored at a given location.  This requirement is only likely to affect Pacorini at Vlissingen, where they operate 40 of 42 warehouses, and

Metro at Detroit, who operate 29 of 37 warehouses there. Even at 3,000t per day, a backlog of one metal on the scale seen at Detroit or Vlissingen is still capable of trapping other metals for extended periods.  At all other locations, a combination of either lower stock levels or a larger number of operating companies suggests that few, if any, operators must operate at the next step down on the scale of 2,500t per day for stocks of 600,000-900,000t.  It is likely that most warehouses are, in fact, operating at minimum load-out rates of 1,500 or 2,000t per day. 

The LME has now proposed to introduce a further amendment to the minimum load-out rule from 1 April 2013, which looks set to minimise the impact that the vast aluminium stocks have on the other LME metals.  When the queue of one metal reaches 30,000t – a 10-20 day queue depending upon the minimum load-out rate in force – then a further 500t per day of other metals must also be delivered out if the owner has asked for delivery.  This rule, enabling ‘trapped’ metals to jump the queue of aluminium, looks likely to solve the immediate problem.  For example, if all LME copper were in one warehouse and trapped behind a queue of aluminium, with this new rule all of the copper could be shipped out in approximately 80 days. 

A loophole does remain though, as warehouses could potentially seek to play this rule by using large zinc stocks to ‘block’ the new queue, thus trapping copper, lead or nickel.  In light of their actions earlier in the year to prevent apparent stockpiling of copper at Vlissingen behind queues of aluminium, it appears likely that the LME will respond unfavourably to any obvious attempts to do this, but it does nevertheless remain a risk. 

#### **Growth in LME stocks has accelerated in recent years** 

The volume of stock of a metal held at an LME warehouse and the size of the market in that metal are important factors that affect the strain that a given metal can put on the LME warehouse system.  The percentage of global stocks of a metal held by LME registered warehouses is also important.  These three facto

rs in combination define how much metal LME warehouses may have to absorb during times of market surplus or ship out in times of deficit. Once the size of these stocks becomes large, there is scope for extended queues to develop, as has been observed with aluminium. |**Reported metal s**|**tocks and share in LM**

The growth in LME aluminium stocks since 2008 was only possible because of a very large oversupply of the metal. In the period between 2007 and 2012 there has been at least one year where each of the metals aluminium, copper, zinc, and nickel has had a surplus which is greater than 5% of annual demand. For zinc and aluminium these large surpluses were sustained for a long period, yet it is aluminium that dominates stock holdings at LME warehouses. Aluminium oversupply has had such a significant impact because the aluminium market is so much larger than that of other LME metals. In addition, aluminium stocks are disproportionately held within the LME warehouse system as opposed to being held more evenly across a range of producers, consumers and other exchanges. Current global stocks of aluminium are 7Mt, accounting for 15% of annual demand, approximately 5Mt (72% of global stocks) of which are held in LME warehouses. The sheer scale of aluminium stocks inevitably puts pressure on the warehouse system as a whole – even without concentration of stocks in any single location. For copper and nickel, which already have a smaller market size than aluminium and a smaller percentage of demand held as stocks, diversification of stock holdings in different locations further eases pressure on the LME warehouse system. Only 31% of global copper stocks are held by LME warehouses, with a further 24% in the hands of producers and 23% held by the SHFE **.** This diversification enables consumers to turn to other sources of metal should queues for material from LME warehouses become untenable. With both of these metals, the distribution of stocks has remained broadly in line with what has been observed over the past decade. While this represents a return to sizeable stock levels for zinc, the percentage of aluminium stocks at LME warehouses is a continuation of a notably high level of inventory. Since the aluminium market returned to surplus in 2007, IAI and Japanese merchant consumer stock have remained relatively constant and currently total about 1.5Mt. Stocks held by the SHFE have risen from a low of 16,000t in Q3 2006 to 400,000t in Q3 2012. In the same period, LME stocks have risen from 690,000t to over 5Mt. Clearly the scale of the aluminium market and not just the existence of a large oversupply of aluminium is a major factor. #### **Regional and local concentration of LME stocks has occurred** The absolute size of LME stocks and their scale relative to other global stocks has been a driving force behind the queues of aluminium seeking to leave warehouses, but the additional effect of metals becoming concentrated in a given location cannot be underestimated. If stocks are well diversified across numerous LME warehouse locations, large stocks of material should not pose a problem. This, however, is not the case. Global aluminium and zinc stocks are not just concentrated within LME registered warehouses, but at a few locations within this

On a regional basis, stocks in US warehouses grew strongly throughout the period from 2008 to 2012. Stocks in Asian warehouses grew steadily to January 2010, but have remained stable, or even declined since then. In Europe, the stocks in warehouses have grown almost as much as those in the US over the same period, but far more erratically. There has been, during October and November 2012, a sharp spike in European LME stocks, with the addition of almost half a million tonnes in the one month period (155kt each of aluminium and zinc, 105kt of lead and 27kt of copper). Focussing upon specific locations, there are a few that hold a large percentage of total LME warehouse stocks of certain metals. Almost 30% of LME aluminium stocks are held in Detroit, which also holds about 15% of lead and 10% of zinc stocks. A further 25% of LME aluminium stocks reside at Vlissingen, alongside more than 5% of lead and nickel stocks. Since 2009, zinc stocks at New Orleans have increased from 63,000t (then 25% of LME zinc stocks) to 724,000t (62% of LME zinc stocks) in November of 2012, in addition to a holding of approximately 20% of copper stocks. For most of these metals, the concentration of stocks in one location is of limited concern – the volumes are just too small for a queue to form. Aluminium stocks are, however, large enough to produce queues. This can be illustrated by the following theoretical example; if an amount of metal equal to 2% of annual demand must be delivered out of LME warehouses annually and at a constant rate, then 2.3Mt of aluminium (almost 9,000t per day, assuming five working days a week) must be shipped from warehouses globally. By contrast, just 980,000t per year (3,800t per day) of copper would require shipping out. If spread across a large number of warehouse locations, these delivery demands could easily be met, particularly with the current minimum load-out rate of 3,000t per day for the largest warehouses. If concentrated in just two warehouses, then a queue would form at the rate of 3,000t per day. By contrast, two warehouses holding copper would be able to deliver the material without queues forming. #### **Cancelled stock can indicate development of queues** The cancelling of a warrant – asking a warehouse to ship your metal – marks the point at which an owner starts waiting for the delivery of their metal. Sustained increases in cancelled warrants indicates one of two things, a surge in physical demand for the metal or long queues as owners request their metal at a rate faster than the warehouse’s minimum unloading rate. Reported stock within LME warehouses consists of open tonnage and cancelled tonnage. Cancelled stock is metal which the owner has cancelled the warrant on and is either awaiting delivery of the material out of the warehouse or awaiting re-issue of warrants. As it is assumed that a relatively small percentage of cancelled sto

ck is awaiting re-issue of warrants, large volumes of cancelled stock at a given location indicate queues for delivery out of that warehouse. Similarly, growing volumes of cancelled stock indicate growing queues at that location. In November 2012, cancelled warrants accounted for 36% of total LME stocks. Aluminium cancelled tonnage accounted for about 10% of total aluminium warehouse stocks up until December 2011. In a period of just two months, cancelled tonnage jumped to 25% of total LME aluminium stocks. Since that date cancelled tonnage has remained stubbornly high and has risen to its current level of 36% of aluminium stocks. Around the same time, there was a surge in aluminium delivered into LME warehouses, pushing up total aluminium stocks. Almost 50% of the apparent queue at New Orleans emerged over just three working days from 14 to 19 September 2012 as cancelled stock increased nearly five-fold due to surges in

cancelled warrants on copper and zinc. Since then cancelled stocks of zinc held at New Orleans has continued to increase, reaching 53% of New Orleans zinc stocks and 33% of global LME zinc stocks by 1 November. As noted previously, this backlog will take over 100 working days to clear if metal continues to be moved at current rates. About 30,000 tonnes of copper are somewhere in this queue, whilst a further 20,000 tonnes (8% of LME stocks, but under 3% of global stocks) of open tonnage remain yet to join the queue. These queues essentially reduce the physical availability of metal, tightening the market despite the presence of metal in the warehouses. #### **Queues can affect LME stocks, but not other stocks** At present stock levels, and with the relative usage of the LME by the five metals considered in this report, it is unlikely that copper, lead, or nickel could create the backlogs observed in the LME warehouse system, even if all LME stocks of these metals were concentrated in one location. Global cancelled tonnage of the three metals combined is less than half of the cancelled tonnage of zinc at New Orleans alone and less than a quarter of the cancelled tonnage of aluminium at either Detroit or Vlissingen. © 2012 CRU International Limited **confidential** Page 11 of 16 Copper Studies November 2012 www.crugroup.com The risk for these metals is that they become ‘trapped’ behind the long queues for aluminium and zinc, due to stocks being concentrated in locations where large queues have formed. As of November 2012, five warehouse locations are estimated to have queues of over five weeks for delivery of metal. These are Detroit, Vlissingen, New Orleans, Antwerp and Johor. The stocks of nickel and copper in these LME warehouses are in the region of 10% of global stocks and so should have limited impact upon supply or prices unless there is a considerable supply shock. Aluminium held in these warehouses is 51% of total LME stocks and 37% of global aluminium stocks and is concentrated in Detroit and Vlissingen, which have the longest queues. Just under 38% of global lead stocks are held in LME warehouses with queues, however, two-thirds of this is at Antwerp and Johor, where the queues are shorter than at the other three locations. sponse to queues** Premiums paid for physical metal should primarily be influenced by regional supply and demand. In an oversupplied market, premiums should be low, while as a market tightens, premiums should increase. © 2012 CRU International Limited **confidential** Page 14 of 16 November 2012 Copper Studies www.crugroup.com #### **Financing and forward selling can result in lack of readily available metal** Apart from the purely volumetric considerations outlined above, the other factor that has been put forward to explain the lack of availability of metal in LME warehouses relates to financial transactions. There are two financial approaches which are cited as reasons for material being tied up; forward-selling by market participants looking to make returns as they ‘roll-up’ the forward curve; and financing of metal – that is the use of stored metal as collateral against loans. The trading strategy of buying spot aluminium and selling forward during a large contango is quoted as the catalyst for the initial growth in aluminium stocks held at LME warehouses – although it must be remembered that the considerable oversupply had to go somewhere. With this approach, the forwardseller buys the metal today and, at the expiry of the forward contract, receives today’s forward price from the purchaser, but must repay any storage and borrowing costs. If the market is in contango, and the contango is sufficiently large, the forward seller can make a return from this activity. Calculations using historic data indicate that between 2000 and 2006 returns from this strategy were rarely positive, with the exception of copper. Through this period, copper, zinc, and nickel experienced days where large annualised returns were possible, but also numerous days, and longer periods, where annualised losses could exceed 5% or even 10%. From May 2006 to June 2009 aluminium, by contrast, exhibited a large and prolonged contango, which made positive returns possible. Since 2009, however, forward selling has rarely been profitable and, when it was, offered low returns. The other activity that can tie-up metal for long periods of time is financing.

This involves a company using metal deposited in a warehouse as collateral against a loan.  With warehouses able to offer incentives due to the long queues and resultant strong rental income, metal can easily be attracted.  Of concern for the future is whether exchange-traded funds (ETFs) will reduce availability of metal stocks, and push up premiums, should they grow to a large enough size.  Copper ETFs proposed by JP Morgan Chase and Blackrock would require an amount of copper equivalent to 25% of reported global stocks or just over 80% of LME stocks.  This metal would then remain locked away from the physical market, with the potential to push up premiums for physical metal. 

#### **Winners and losers** 

The development of queues within the LME warehouse system has had a differential impact on the various LME metal markets and on the various participants within those markets.  The aluminium industry has experienced the greatest impact, as the large volumes of aluminium held in LME warehouses are the main block on warehouse deliveries from certain locations.  Rising premiums and lack of availability of metal from the LME, despite high stocks, is a major issue in this market.  Zinc has also been adversely affected by the appearance of queues while other metals, including copper, have been influenced to a much lesser extent. 

In terms of market participants, it would appear that producers have been benefiting from the elevated level of premiums prevailing in the market and it is possible that traders may do so in the future too. However, this assumes that delivered prices have remained strictly LME plus the relevant premium.  If

any increase in premiums has been met by a discounted LME price, then producers and traders may not have seen margins inflate as much as appears at first sight. 

Of course, the hike in premiums has caused the greatest problems for consumers. Premiums are generally less transparent than the LME price and consequently cannot easily be passed on to customers.  Equally importantly, an increase in premiums cannot be hedged in the same way as the LME price thereby potentially leading to reduced margins for semi-fabricators.  The combination of these factors meant purchasers of aluminium ingot were reluctant to quickly agree 2013 contracts, hoping instead to agree lower premiums than had initially been tabled. 

Copper is, alongside nickel, one of the two LME metals which appear relatively unaffected by the current queues.  When the LME de-listed Vlissingen as a destination for LME copper deliveries it was because of concern that copper stocks could become trapped and consequently that premiums would spike.  Looking ahead, copper stocks look relatively safe from troubles in LME warehouses, even more so should the 500t per day additional load-out rule come into operation. 

With just 31% of global copper s

tocks in LME warehouses, LME stocks do not appear as important a source of supply in the copper market as they are in aluminium or zinc.  Of course, this could potentially change should large volumes of oversupply develop, which become concentrated in a few LME warehouse locations.  For the time being, however, this appears unlikely.  The copper market surplus expected next year, at 265,000t, is unlikely to end up entirely in LME warehouses let alone be destined for a few key locations within the LME system.
